title: Crisis Mental Support
summary: Practical techniques to manage acute panic, anxiety, and shock in high-stress disaster situations.

sections.heading: Step 1 — Use the 5-4-3-2-1 Grounding Method
sections.body: When feeling overwhelmed, panic-stricken, or disassociated, ground yourself in the present moment by naming: 5 things you can see around you; 4 things you can physically touch; 3 things you can hear; 2 things you can smell; and 1 thing you can taste. This shifts brain activity away from fight-or-flight.
sections.warning: Ensure you are in a safe physical environment before starting grounding exercises.
sections.image_description: Icons representing eye, hand, ear, nose, and mouth in sequence

sections.heading: Step 2 — Practice Box Breathing
sections.body: Regulate your nervous system by slowing down your breath. Use the box breathing technique: 1. Inhale deeply through your nose for 4 seconds. 2. Hold your breath for 4 seconds. 3. Exhale slowly through your mouth for 4 seconds. 4. Hold your lungs empty for 4 seconds. Repeat this loop 4 to 5 times.
sections.warning: Avoid rapid, shallow breathing (hyperventilation), which can cause dizziness or fainting.
sections.image_description: A square diagram showing inhale, hold, exhale, hold along each edge

sections.heading: Step 3 — Offer Psychological First Aid
sections.body: If helping someone else in shock: 1. Look: check for safety and basic needs. 2. Listen: approach them calmly, ask their name, and listen without forcing them to talk. 3. Link: help them connect with family, medical services, or basic needs. Keep your voice low, steady, and reassuring.
sections.warning: Do not say 'everything will be fine' or give false hope. Validate their feelings instead.
sections.image_description: Two people sitting close, one listening and holding the other's hand

sections.heading: Step 4 — Regain Control via Small Actions
sections.body: Panic often stems from a feeling of helplessness. Regain a sense of control by focusing on small, immediately achievable tasks: organize your survival pack, take a sip of water, sweep the shelter floor, or check on a companion. Small successes rebuild cognitive agency.
sections.warning: Do not attempt to make major, complex decisions while in a state of high panic.
sections.image_description: Person drinking water or organizing a small medical kit

when_to_use: When you or someone else is experiencing an acute anxiety attack, shock, or severe distress during a crisis or disaster.
do_not: Tell a panicking person to 'calm down'
Tell them what they should feel or think
Leave a distressed or shocked person alone
sources: World Health Organization Psychological First Aid Guide
